questions.q: How does Ansible reach managed nodes?
options: Agentless: over SSH, copying a module, running it, collecting JSON and deleting it (no Ansible daemon)
questions.explain: Managed nodes need sshd and Python.

questions.q: Is Ansible push or pull?
options: Push: the control node decides when to run and reaches out
questions.explain: Contrast with pull tools where agents fetch config.

questions.q: What runs Ansible?
options: The control node (a laptop or CI runner) with inventory, playbook and roles
questions.explain: ansible-playbook is the only program.

questions.q: What caveat applies to 'declarative' tasks?
options: Tasks say what should be true, but modules like command can't know state, so idempotency is on you
questions.explain: It's declarative-ish.

questions.q: What is an ad-hoc command?
options: One module run on one or many hosts, e.g. ansible web1 -i hosts.ini -m command -a "echo hello"
questions.explain: -m selects the module and -a its arguments.

questions.q: Why did `echo hello` via the command module report CHANGED?
options: The command module can't know whether anything changed
questions.explain: Idempotency is on you with command/shell.

questions.q: What should module names be written as?
options: Fully qualified collection names such as ansible.builtin.copy
questions.explain: FQCN avoids ambiguity.

questions.q: Which tool documents a module?
questions.explain: It shows parameters and examples offline.

questions.q: What does inventory define?
options: What exists: hosts, groups and variables
questions.explain: INI is compact; YAML suits lists and dictionaries.

questions.q: What does `[prod:children]` with web and db mean?
options: Group prod contains the groups web and db
questions.explain: ansible-inventory --graph confirms the tree.

questions.q: How do you inspect how Ansible understood inventory?
questions.explain: Inspect before you trust.

questions.q: Group variable http_port=80 on [web] and host http_port=8081 on web1: what does web1 get?
questions.explain: The --host output showed 8081 for web1 and 80 for web2.

questions.q: What is a playbook?
options: A YAML list of plays, each mapping hosts to a list of tasks
questions.explain: Tasks run in order on each host.

questions.q: What does gather_facts do?
options: Runs setup to collect host facts before tasks
questions.explain: It can be disabled to save time.

questions.q: Why give tasks names?
options: They appear in output and make runs readable
questions.explain: Unnamed tasks print module names only.

questions.q: What's a common YAML pitfall?
options: Indentation and unquoted special values like colons or booleans
questions.explain: Quote values that YAML might misread.

questions.q: What should the recap show on a repeat run of a converged playbook?
questions.explain: The recap is the instrument for idempotency.

questions.q: Why does an unguarded command task report changed every run?
questions.explain: State-aware modules like file and copy report ok on the second run.

questions.q: How does `creates:` help a command task?
options: If the file exists the command is skipped, making it idempotent
questions.explain: A condition makes the command safe to repeat.

questions.q: What does `changed_when: false` mean on a read-only command?
options: Reading never changes anything, so never report changed
questions.explain: changed_when and failed_when interpret results.

questions.q: What does `{{ missing | default('fallback') }}` do when undefined?
options: Gives 'fallback'; without default an undefined variable is an error
questions.explain: default makes optional values safe.

questions.q: What beats every other variable source?
questions.explain: They override even set_fact.

questions.q: What does set_fact do?
options: Creates or changes a variable for the rest of the play for that host, higher in precedence than play vars
questions.explain: Shown by the debug before and after.

questions.q: Why quote a value starting with {{ in YAML?
questions.explain: Strings with a leading {{ must be quoted.

questions.q: How is a task skipped by `when` reported?
options: skipping, and not counted as changed
questions.explain: when takes a Jinja2 expression without {{ }}.

questions.q: How is `when` evaluated on a looped task?
questions.explain: For example when: item.admin.

questions.q: What does loop_control: {label: ...} do?
options: Shortens the output label per item
questions.explain: It prints item.name instead of the whole dict.

questions.q: What does `ansible_facts.os_family == 'Debian'` target?
questions.explain: On macOS os_family was Darwin, so it skipped.

questions.q: What is a template?
options: A Jinja2 file (.j2) rendered per host into a config file
questions.explain: {{ }} prints values; {% if %} and {% for %} control flow.

questions.q: Why add a managed-by header?
options: So people know hand edits will be reverted
questions.explain: Also keep logic out of templates.

questions.q: What does `validate:` on template or copy do?
options: Checks the file before it replaces the live one
questions.explain: For example validating a config with the service's own checker.

questions.q: When do handlers fire?
options: Once, at the end of the play, only if a notifying task changed
questions.explain: flush_handlers forces them earlier.

questions.q: How should you read an Ansible failure?
options: Top-down: the task, host, module, then what/why/where (file:line:column)
questions.explain: The origin shows the failing line.

questions.q: What does `'x' is undefined` usually mean, and a first step?
options: Missing variable, typo, scope or ungathered fact; use debug: var=x
questions.explain: Check inventory and precedence.

questions.q: What does UNREACHABLE point at?
options: The connection: SSH, host key, network or interpreter; use -vvv and try ssh by hand
questions.explain: FAILED with rc means the command ran and failed.

questions.q: How do you inspect a module's arguments?
questions.explain: For 'Unsupported parameters' errors.

questions.q: Why was the first run ok=6 and the second ok=5 changed=0?
options: The handler ran once on the first run; the second run changed nothing so no handler fired
questions.explain: Convergence: zero changes on repeat.

questions.q: What does blockinfile manage?
options: A block of lines between marker comments, e.g. two sysctl settings
questions.explain: lineinfile edits a single line like PermitRootLogin.

questions.q: What did the drift test show?
options: Hand edits (a bad line, a changed mode) were detected and corrected by re-running the playbook
questions.explain: The tests call the real ansible-playbook.

questions.q: How were the 'servers' simulated?
options: Local directories (node1, node2) with the local connection, so it ran on a laptop
questions.explain: Tests verified results with pytest.

questions.q: What does a role package?
options: Everything to configure one thing: tasks, default variables, templates, files, handlers
questions.explain: ansible-galaxy role init scaffolds the layout.

questions.q: Defaults versus vars in a role?
options: defaults/main.yml holds variables users are meant to override (lowest precedence); vars/main.yml holds internal constants (high precedence)
questions.explain: defaults are the role's public interface.

questions.q: Which file is the role's entry point?
questions.explain: meta/main.yml holds author, platforms and dependencies.

questions.q: Why validate inputs with assert at the start of the role?
options: Fail early with a clear message (e.g. port 1–65535) instead of failing deep inside later tasks
questions.explain: fail_msg explains the expected range.

questions.q: Which source wins above all others?
questions.explain: They beat even set_fact.

questions.q: Which source has the lowest precedence?
questions.explain: That's why defaults are safe to override.

questions.q: Host versus group variables?
options: Host beats group, and a specific group beats all
questions.explain: At both inventory levels.

questions.q: How was the order established?
options: By measurement: a script generated a fresh project per trial, ran the playbook and read which source's value won
questions.explain: 14 sources ranked by experiment.

questions.q: What does `servers | selectattr('port','gt',100) | map(attribute='name') | list` return for ports 80, 8080, 443?
questions.explain: Ports above 100: b and c.

questions.q: Why end with `| list` after map or selectattr?
options: They return generators; list (or join) materialises the result
questions.explain: Otherwise you print a generator object.

questions.q: Shallow versus recursive combine of {a:1,b:{c:2,d:3}} with {b:{c:9},e:5}?
options: Shallow replaces b entirely ({c:9}); recursive=True merges ({c:9, d:3})
questions.explain: Variables from different layers don't merge on their own.

questions.q: What does `'web-01.example.com' | regex_replace('^(\w+)-(\d+).*', '\2:\1')` give?
questions.explain: Groups swapped; mind the backslashes in YAML.

questions.q: What happens by default when a task fails on a host?
options: Ansible stops that host's remaining tasks and continues with other hosts
questions.explain: Blocks, rescue and always change that.

questions.q: What do block, rescue and always do?
options: block groups tasks; on failure the rest are skipped and rescue runs; always runs regardless
questions.explain: In the example 'never reached' was skipped.

questions.q: Is rescue an automatic rollback?
options: No: it runs the tasks you wrote, which must themselves be idempotent and safe
questions.explain: A failing rescue task fails the host, but always still runs.

questions.q: What does ansible_failed_task give inside rescue?
options: Details of the failed task (name, result)
questions.explain: Use it for a precise rollback message.

questions.q: What does an encrypted vault file start with?
questions.explain: Encrypted with ansible-vault encrypt.

questions.q: Does encrypting the same content twice give the same ciphertext?
options: Only with the same salt file
questions.explain: Random salt is used.

questions.q: What happens with a wrong vault password?
options: Decryption failed (no vault secrets were found that could decrypt)
questions.explain: No secret supplied gives a different error.

questions.q: What does ansible-vault rekey do?
options: Changes the password without changing the contents
questions.explain: Use --vault-password-file.

questions.q: What does ansible-core contain?
options: The engine and ansible.builtin modules and plugins; everything else lives in collections
questions.explain: 71 builtin modules on the lesson's install.

questions.q: What are the parts of a fully qualified collection name?
questions.explain: Install collections via ansible-galaxy.

questions.q: What happens with an unknown module/action?
options: The whole play aborts at load time; ignore_errors doesn't help
questions.explain: Resolution errors are precise.

questions.q: How do you pin collection versions for a project?
options: A requirements.yml file installed with ansible-galaxy
questions.explain: Dependencies should be reproducible.

questions.q: What does `--tags configure` run?
options: configure tasks plus tasks tagged always
questions.explain: always runs unless skipped.

questions.q: What does a task tagged `never` do with no options?
options: It doesn't run unless asked via its other tag
questions.explain: --tags debug_only runs it.

questions.q: Which tasks run with no options?
options: Untagged and tagged tasks alike, except those tagged never
questions.explain: install, configure, always and untagged ran.

questions.q: What does --limit do?
options: Restricts which hosts the play targets
questions.explain: Combine with tags and check mode to target one change on one host.

questions.q: What does delegate_to do?
options: Runs the task on another host while keeping the original host's variable context
questions.explain: For example draining a host from a load balancer via lb1.

questions.q: What's a delegation gotcha?
options: Parallel delegated tasks against one host can race; facts attach to the delegated host only with delegate_facts
questions.explain: command isn't a shell, so $(...) printed literally.

questions.q: What does run_once do?
options: Runs a task on one host in the batch instead of every host
questions.explain: Useful for migrations.

questions.q: Why use serial batches?
options: Roll changes through hosts in small groups, with max_fail_percentage to stop on problems
questions.explain: They limit blast radius.

questions.q: What does ansible-playbook --syntax-check do?
options: Parses the playbook without connecting, catching YAML and structural errors
questions.explain: The first rung of the testing ladder.

questions.q: What does ansible-lint's `no-changed-when` flag?
options: command/shell without changed_when, which breaks idempotency reporting
questions.explain: Others: fqcn, name, no-free-form, package-latest.

questions.q: Why does `state: latest` get flagged?
questions.explain: Pin versions or use present.

questions.q: What are lint profiles?
options: Rule sets from basic to production that a playbook can meet
questions.explain: The fixed playbook passed 'production'.

questions.q: What does the webapp role's interface consist of?
options: defaults/main.yml variables (port, workers, root), with internal constants in vars/main.yml, documented in a README
questions.explain: The role has validation and a handler.

questions.q: What does the 'idempotent' test assert?
options: A second run exits 0 and changed=0 for every host
questions.explain: Using real ansible-playbook runs.

questions.q: What does the 'invalid port fails before changing anything' test show?
options: Validation with assert stops early with a non-zero exit and a clear message
questions.explain: webapp_port=70000 is rejected.

questions.q: What does the check-mode test assert?
options: --check exits 0 and writes nothing (the output directory isn't created)
questions.explain: Nine tests all passed.

questions.q: When should you write a custom module?
options: When no module does what you need and command would be fragile
questions.explain: A module is a Python program.

questions.q: How does a module report results?
options: exit_json on success and fail_json on failure
questions.explain: Plus an argument spec, check mode and diff support.

questions.q: Why support check mode in a module?
options: So --check reports what would change without changing it
questions.explain: Be honest about 'changed'.

questions.q: What's the argument spec?
options: A declaration of parameters, types, defaults and required fields that Ansible validates
questions.explain: It makes invalid input fail clearly.

questions.q: What is a filter plugin?
options: A Python file with a FilterModule class whose filters() returns a dict of names to functions
questions.explain: Placed in filter_plugins/ next to the playbook or inside a role/collection.

questions.q: Which design points matter?
options: Pure functions, native return types, validated inputs raising AnsibleFilterError, no mutation of arguments, documentation
questions.explain: mask_secrets returns a copy.

questions.q: What do lookups do versus filters?
options: Lookups fetch data from outside the play (file, environment); filters transform data inside expressions
questions.explain: The lesson wrote an envfile lookup.

questions.q: What does the mask_secrets filter mask?
options: Values whose keys look sensitive (password, secret, token)
questions.explain: Including nested dictionaries.

questions.q: Why do static inventories rot?
options: Servers are created and destroyed by autoscalers faster than a hand-edited file can track
questions.explain: Use a source of truth like a CMDB.

questions.q: What must an inventory script print for --list?
options: Valid JSON including _meta hostvars, exit code 0; it also answers --host NAME
questions.explain: _meta avoids one call per host.

questions.q: In the CSV example, which groups does web-01 belong to?
questions.explain: Each row becomes a host in two groups.

questions.q: What are the two ways shown to build dynamic inventory?
options: An inventory script and an inventory plugin
questions.explain: Plugins can also cache results.

questions.q: What can `command` NOT do?
options: Pipes, redirection, &&, $(...) and globbing, since there's no shell
questions.explain: shell runs through /bin/sh.

questions.q: What is the safest form of command?
options: argv: a list where each element is one argument with no shell or splitting
questions.explain: `argv: [echo, "a b", "c;d"]` printed a b c;d.

questions.q: How do you prevent injection through variables in shell?
options: The quote filter: `echo {{ evil | quote }}` treats it as data
questions.explain: Without it `ok; echo INJECTED` ran a second command.

questions.q: What are raw and script for?
options: raw sends text over SSH without Python (bootstrapping); script copies and runs a local script
questions.explain: Last-resort tools.

questions.q: Why use async?
options: A long task shouldn't hold the connection open for its entire life (large downloads, long jobs)
questions.explain: The task is started and checked later.

questions.q: What does `poll: 0` mean?
options: Fire and forget: don't wait for the job
questions.explain: Check later with async_status.

questions.q: What does async_status do?
options: Checks a started job's status, typically with retries until finished
questions.explain: Use `until` with retries and delay.

questions.q: What does `async:` set?
options: The maximum time the job may run
questions.explain: poll sets how often Ansible checks.

questions.q: What does `forks` control, and what's the default?
options: Parallel worker processes handling hosts; default 5
questions.explain: Measured: 1 fork 50.1 s, 5 forks 11.1 s, 10 forks 6.6 s, 20 forks 4.5 s on 20 hosts.

questions.q: When do more forks stop helping?
options: When forks reaches the host count; each fork is also a Python process using memory
questions.explain: Scaling is near linear until then.

questions.q: What is gather_facts' hidden cost?
options: It runs the setup module on every host at the start of each play (about 2.3 s vs 0.4 s without, on 20 hosts)
questions.explain: Turn it off or use gather_subset or fact caching.

questions.q: What does the free strategy help with?
options: Slow hosts holding others up at each task under linear
questions.explain: Under linear a slow host delays everyone per task.

questions.q: What does `serial: [1, "50%", "100%"]` give on eight hosts?
options: Batches of 1, 4 and 3: a canary, then half, then the rest
questions.explain: The first is the canary.

questions.q: What's the principle 'drain first, re-enable last'?
options: Remove the host from rotation before changing it, and return it only after it passes the smoke test (always section)
questions.explain: Capacity stays up.

questions.q: What does 'roll back locally, then fail loudly' mean?
options: The rescue restores the previous version on that host, logs it, then fails the host so the batch is marked failed
questions.explain: any_errors_fatal stops the rollout.

questions.q: What's a failure budget?
options: How many failures a rollout tolerates (e.g. max_fail_percentage) before stopping
questions.explain: A bad change is stopped early.

questions.q: Why does removing a task leave legacy.conf on the host?
options: Ansible keeps no state: it has no record that it created the file
questions.explain: Terraform would remove it; Ansible does nothing.

questions.q: What is Fix 1 for orphans?
options: An explicit removal task (state: absent), kept until every environment has run it
questions.explain: Track it in a changelog.

questions.q: What is Fix 2?
options: An allow-list purge: find files in a directory and delete everything not in the managed list
questions.explain: In --check it showed what would be deleted without deleting.

questions.q: What can happen when two tasks fight each other?
options: They keep undoing each other's change every run, so changed never reaches zero
questions.explain: The flip.yml experiment.

questions.q: What protocols manage Windows hosts?
options: WinRM or PSRP (the control node must be Linux or macOS)
questions.explain: ansible.windows ships 81 modules in the lesson's version.

questions.q: How honest is the lesson about verification?
options: No Windows host, network device or API was available, so nothing was executed against them; it's based on documentation and ansible-doc
questions.explain: It says so up front.

questions.q: What connection type do network devices use?
questions.explain: The device has no Python to run modules on.

questions.q: For non-Windows targets, which module should you use instead of win_copy?
questions.explain: As the module doc states.

questions.q: What does the kvfile module manage?
options: key=value entries: state present ensures one line for the key; absent removes it
questions.explain: It preserves comments and unrelated settings.

questions.q: Why a pure apply(lines, key, value, state) function?
options: Only it decides what changes, making it easy to test; main() wires AnsibleModule and file operations
questions.explain: 25 tests cover it.

questions.q: What do check and diff mode do in kvfile?
options: Check never writes; diff returns before and after content
questions.explain: Atomic writes avoid half-written files.

questions.q: Which sequence of changed flags did the playbook show: set, set again, change to 8, remove?
questions.explain: The second set was idempotent.

questions.q: What does a controller (AWX/AAP) add beyond ansible-playbook?
options: Projects, inventories, credentials, job templates, RBAC, scheduling, workflows, history/logging, API, and execution isolation
questions.explain: For teams: who may run what against which hosts.

questions.q: What is the most valuable credential feature?
options: Separation: an operator can use a credential to launch a job without ever seeing its secret
questions.explain: Credentials are encrypted stores.

questions.q: How do AWX and AAP relate?
options: AWX is the upstream open-source project; AAP is Red Hat's commercial product built on it
questions.explain: The lesson notes nothing was installed or run.

questions.q: What do execution environments provide?
options: Jobs run in separate containers rather than on a shared shell
questions.explain: Built with ansible-builder.

questions.q: Why order the pipeline 'cheapest check first'?
options: Run the fastest, most likely-to-fail checks first to fail early
questions.explain: syntax-check, lint, secret hygiene, converge, idempotence, check mode.

questions.q: What does the idempotence step catch?
options: A non-idempotent task: the second run must report changed=0
questions.explain: The nanosecond-writing task made changed=1 each run and failed the step.

questions.q: What does the check-mode step verify?
questions.explain: The last rung.

questions.q: What does the secret hygiene step check?
options: Tasks using secret variables have no_log
questions.explain: A custom linter (nologlint.py).

questions.q: Why use an executable vault password script in CI?
options: A file is awkward; the script reads an environment variable and prints the password, failing closed if it's missing
questions.explain: Missing variable: the script exits 1 and Ansible errors.

questions.q: What does 'fails closed' mean here?
options: A missing secret stops the run rather than proceeding unprotected
questions.explain: The error was 'Vault password script returned non-zero'.

questions.q: How do you keep separate secrets per environment?
questions.explain: A single repository can hold both.

questions.q: What does no_log protect?
options: Secrets appearing in task output and logs at run time
questions.explain: Vault protects at rest; no_log protects output.

questions.q: What does ansible-pull do?
options: The host pulls its own configuration from Git and runs it locally
questions.explain: It's the opposite of push.

questions.q: What does 'only if changed' mean?
options: It runs the playbook only when the repository has new commits (unless forced)
questions.explain: Saves work on unchanged repos.

questions.q: Which hosts suit pull mode?
options: Many hosts that can't be reached from a controller, or that bootstrap themselves
questions.explain: It scales without a push controller.

questions.q: How does pull mode repair drift?
options: By re-running periodically (e.g. cron), reapplying the desired state
questions.explain: The lesson showed drift repair.

questions.q: What is the division of labour?
options: Ansible for infrastructure; Terraform for config
Terraform for networks, VMs, load balancers, databases, DNS; Ansible for OS packages, config, users, services and deployment steps
questions.explain: Neither tool is a secret store.

questions.q: What if both tools create the same cloud resources?
options: They'll fight: pick one owner per resource
questions.explain: The overlap is a trap.

questions.q: Name a handoff pattern.
options: terraform output -json feeding an inventory, or an Ansible cloud inventory plugin (aws_ec2, azure_rm) querying tagged instances
questions.explain: A community plugin can also read state.

questions.q: How honest is the lesson?
options: Terraform wasn't installed, so no apply ran; the handoff logic was built and tested without state
questions.explain: It states what wasn't run.

questions.q: Why not parse console output for drift?
options: It's for humans, mixing headers, items, diffs and warnings; use a callback plugin that writes JSON
questions.explain: The driftreport plugin records changed results.

questions.q: How does the runner audit drift?
options: Runs the playbook with --check --diff and the plugin enabled, then reports with exit codes
questions.explain: Exit 0 means no drift.

questions.q: What must you set to enable the callback plugin?
questions.explain: The aggregate plugin needs enabling.

questions.q: What is drift?
options: The difference between what automation says and what a machine actually has
questions.explain: Check mode reveals it without changing anything.

questions.q: Why does automation 'multiply mistakes as well as effort'?
options: One wrong hosts: pattern or bad variable changes every targeted host at once
questions.explain: Control blast radius.

questions.q: Which control addresses 'wrong target'?
options: A preflight guard, protected groups and limits
questions.explain: The tested preflight.py computes the blast radius first.

questions.q: Which control addresses 'batch too large'?
options: serial, failure budget and tested abort semantics
questions.explain: 200 hosts restarted at once is the example.

questions.q: How can a scheduled drift repair cause an incident?
options: It reverts an emergency hot patch; audit drift before applying
questions.explain: Review drift first.

questions.q: Why isn't the provisioning script idempotent?
options: mkdir fails if the directory exists (set -e exits 1), and >> appends port=8080 again on re-run
questions.explain: It's correct only from one starting state and only once.

questions.q: What does the playbook equivalent give?
options: State-aware modules that converge: reruns change nothing
questions.explain: Compare repeated runs.

questions.q: What happened without set -e after two runs?
questions.explain: The script 'worked' silently wrong.

questions.q: What's the migration lesson?
options: Don't just wrap scripts in shell tasks: use modules and desired state, or idempotency is still on you
questions.explain: Avoid anti-patterns.

questions.q: Why write standards down and enforce them with tools?
options: With ten authors quality drifts; a rule with an automated check is enforced, one nobody can check is ignored
questions.explain: Keep rules few and checkable.

questions.q: Which standards belong in the one-pager?
options: Layout, naming, modules (FQCN), variables, safety (no_log, assert, serial), testing, pinned versions, documentation, release tagging
questions.explain: Nine areas.

questions.q: What are ansible-lint profiles?
options: Rule sets of increasing strictness (min, basic, moderate, safety, shared, production)
questions.explain: Choose by risk.

questions.q: What do warn_list and skip_list do?
options: warn_list reports without failing the build; skip_list isn't checked at all
questions.explain: A ratchet tightens over time.

questions.q: What does the capstone fleet consist of?
options: A simulated 12-node fleet (web01–08, db01–04) with generated inventory and local connections
questions.explain: No remote hosts, SSH or privilege escalation were involved.

questions.q: What did the idempotence step assert?
options: Second run changed=0 on all 12 nodes
questions.explain: After the first converge of changed=6 on every node.

questions.q: What did the preflight step refuse?
options: `all` (exceeds --max-hosts 5) and a single production node without confirmation
questions.explain: Blast-radius control.

questions.q: What did the targeted repair do?
options: With --limit web03,db02,web07 only those three hosts ran and changed, leaving the rest untouched
questions.explain: Then a clean audit exited 0.

questions.q:
A playbook reports `changed=1` on every run for this task. Why?
```yaml
- ansible.builtin.command: echo hi
```
options: command can't know state, so it reports changed every time; add changed_when: false (read-only) or creates:/guards
questions.explain: State-aware modules like file and copy report ok on repeat runs.

questions.q: Which task is idempotent?
questions.explain: mkdir fails when it exists, and >> appends duplicates.

questions.q: On a repeat run of a converged playbook, what should the recap show?
questions.explain: The recap is the instrument.

questions.q: `http_port` is 80 in [web:vars], 8081 on host web1, and web1 runs with `-e http_port=9000`. Which wins for web1?
questions.explain: Host beats group and extra vars beat both (measured precedence).

questions.q: A role's defaults/main.yml sets webapp_port: 8080 and a play passes webapp_port: 9000 as a role parameter. What happens?
options: The role parameter overrides the default, since defaults have the lowest precedence
questions.explain: defaults are the role's public interface.

questions.q: `servers | selectattr('port','gt',100) | map(attribute='name') | list` with ports 80, 8080, 443 (names a, b, c) returns:
questions.explain: Ports above 100: 8080 and 443.

questions.q: Shallow versus recursive combine of {a:1, b:{c:2, d:3}} with {b:{c:9}, e:5}.
options: Shallow: {a:1, b:{c:9}, e:5}; recursive=True: {a:1, b:{c:9, d:3}, e:5}
questions.explain: A plain combine replaces whole values for matching keys.

questions.q: A handler is notified by three tasks that each changed. How often does it run?
options: Once, at the end of the play
questions.explain: Handlers fire once per play unless flushed.

questions.q: A task with `when: ansible_facts.os_family == 'Debian'` runs on macOS. What's reported?
options: skipping: not counted as changed (os_family is Darwin)
questions.explain: Skipped tasks aren't changed.

questions.q: Which structure runs a health check and rolls back on failure but always cleans up?
questions.explain: Rescue runs only when the block fails; always runs regardless.

questions.q: What does `serial: [1, "50%", "100%"]` produce on eight hosts?
options: Batches of 1, 4 and 3: a canary, then half, then the rest
questions.explain: Verified by arithmetic: 1, then 50% of 8 = 4, then the remaining 3.

questions.q: An 'UNREACHABLE' error indicates what, and what's the first step?
options: A connection problem (SSH, host key, network or interpreter); use -vvv and try ssh by hand
questions.explain: FAILED with rc= means the command ran and failed.

questions.q: `command: echo {{ user_input }}` is run with user_input 'ok; rm -rf x' under shell. How do you make it safe?
options: Use `{{ user_input | quote }}` (or avoid shell and pass argv)
questions.explain: The variable text is pasted into the shell line.

questions.q: A task removed from the playbook leaves its file on every host. Why?
options: Ansible keeps no state: it has no record it created the file, so add an explicit state: absent task or an allow-list purge
questions.explain: Terraform would destroy it; Ansible won't.

questions.q: Which command encrypts a secrets file, and what does the file start with?
questions.explain: Encrypting twice gives different ciphertext.

questions.q: How do you restrict a run to one task group on one host?
questions.explain: Combine with --check to preview.

questions.q: A scheduled pipeline must show whether any host has drifted without changing anything. What do you run?
options: The playbook with --check --diff, reporting changed tasks (exit non-zero on drift)
questions.explain: Check mode is the drift audit.

questions.q: A second CI run of a new playbook reports changed=1 because a task writes the current time into a file. What does the pipeline do?
options: Fail the idempotence step, since the task would flap on every run in production
questions.explain: Idempotence is a CI gate.

questions.q: Which tool owns creating VMs and load balancers, and which owns OS config and deployment steps?
options: Terraform owns infrastructure; Ansible owns on-host config and orchestration
questions.explain: Pick one owner per resource.

challenges.title: Render a config template
challenges.prompt: Write the Jinja2 template that renders an nginx-style server block: a managed-by header, listen port, server_name (appending .example.com only when env is 'production') and one comment line per upstream with loop.index, name and weight defaulting to 1. Print the staging render, then the production server_name line. (Needs Jinja2: pip install jinja2.)
challenges.starter:
from jinja2 import Environment
env = Environment(trim_blocks=True, lstrip_blocks=True)
TEMPLATE = """# TODO: write the Jinja2 template: managed-by header, listen port,
# server_name (add .example.com when env == 'production'), and one comment per upstream
# with loop.index, name and weight (default 1)
"""
vars_ = {"http_port": 8081, "inventory_hostname": "web1", "env": "staging",
         "upstreams": [{"name": "a", "weight": 3}, {"name": "b"}]}
print(env.from_string(TEMPLATE).render(**vars_), end="")
vars_["env"] = "production"
print(env.from_string(TEMPLATE).render(**vars_).splitlines()[3])
challenges.explain: Ansible's template module uses Jinja2, so {{ }} prints values, {% if %} and {% for %} control flow, and the default filter handles optional weights. Verified by running the solution with Jinja2.
